name: Translation With Human Review
title: Translation With Human Review
answer: Translation tools let schools reach families in many languages, but they are not perfect and errors can matter. The practical rule is to use machine translation for routine messages and human review for critical ones, such as safety incidents, disciplinary hearings, or special education meetings. Schools should name reviewers for each major home language in the community.

sections.body: Translation tools make it possible to reach families in dozens of languages, and tools like TalkingPoints translate messages in both directions while Microsoft Translator handles documents and speech. These tools have opened communication with families who were once left out. They are not perfect, and the errors can matter. The idea of translation with human review is to treat machine translation as a first draft for routine messages while ensuring a fluent person checks anything critical before it is sent. This solves the problem of reaching more families without letting translation mistakes carry serious consequences.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the rule is to match the tool to the message. A reminder about picture day can go out through a translation tool without further review. A notice about a safety incident, a disciplinary hearing, or a special education meeting should be reviewed by a fluent person before it is sent. Districts should name reviewers for each major home language in the community so that review is available when it is needed. The text does not give grade band differences for this practice.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research from health care. A review of 27 studies found that machine translation works best on simple sentences and in widely spoken European languages, and recommended treating it as a first draft to be corrected by a person (Dew et al., 2018). A review of 18 studies found serious errors in a majority of them, with accuracy lower for languages such as Haitian Creole and Vietnamese (Strechen et al., 2025). The text states that schools face the same limits.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Machine translation is not perfect and the errors can matter, so it should not be the final step for critical messages. A fluent person must review notices about safety incidents, disciplinary hearings, and special education meetings before they are sent. Districts should name reviewers for each major home language in the community. Schools' legal duties to families with limited English continue even as federal guidance has changed, and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act still applies to how schools serve English learners and their families (Hardin, 2025). Districts should check their state requirements for translation and interpretation.
